description:
Blazing-fast Claude in your terminal — a C++26 alternative to claude-code.

agentty is a native C++26 terminal coding agent and a drop-in alternative to claude-code. A single static binary with sub-millisecond cold start, sandboxed by default, and one-command SSH air-gap. No Node, Python, or Electron. Signs in with your Claude Pro/Max subscription or an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
Added
- The agent can ask you to choose. When a request is ambiguous or a
  decision is yours (which design, whether to delete something), the model
  can stop and ask up to four multiple-choice questions in a card under the
  turn. It starts on the model's suggestion (★); pick with the arrows and
  Enter or a digit, tick several with Space where it allows, or type your
  own answer in the usual message box and press Enter. Several questions get
  tabs and a review page before anything is sent. Esc stops the turn, as it
  does mid-reply. The finished card keeps question →
  answer in the transcript.
  Like OpenCode's question and Claude Code's AskUserQuestion. Don't want
  it? Ctrl+K → Settings → Ask clarifying questions turns it off entirely:
  the tool is no longer offered to the model. It never appears in
  agentty run, ACP sessions or subagents, where nobody could answer.
Security
- MCP servers, ACP agents and retrieval helpers run in the sandbox. They
  used to start with your full authority — an npx some-mcp-server could
  read ~/.ssh, ~/.aws and every repo, and reach your LAN. Now each gets
  walls for what it is: MCP servers get the workspace and the proxied
  network; ACP agents also get their own sign-in directory (and only their
  own); retrieval helpers get a read-only workspace and no network. With the
  sandbox on, a server that cannot be sandboxed is refused with the reason,
  never started without one. Linux; macOS and Windows next.
- Nothing agentty runs can change agentty's own config. ~/.agentty
  holds the sandbox policy, the MCP servers, hooks and agents that start
  without asking, and the approval store. The agent's file tools now refuse
  to write, delete or move anything there under every Trust handoff setting,
  allow included, and through symlinks; sandboxed commands see it
  read-only even with the workspace at $HOME. Writing another agent's
  server list (.mcp.json, ~/.claude.json, .codex/, .gemini/,
  .junie/) is now a trust handoff too.
- The sandbox says what it stopped and what this host can't do. Files a
  command was refused now appear in the Sandbox pane's blocked list by path
  (only ones you could have written yourself). On a host without user
  namespaces the banner names what is missing in words — "other processes:
  visible", "protected files: tool gate only" — and the model is told what
  that means for its commands. On Linux 6.15+ the kernel's audit log records
  each denial too.
- The sandbox works, and holds, on hosts without user namespaces. Ubuntu
  24.04's AppArmor default denies them, and on such a host every sandboxed
  command failed to start; underneath that, a masked .env could be read in
  full and "network: Full" meant the open host network. Now, with Landlock
  alone: secrets stay masked, read-only paths like .vscode/tasks.json and
  .git/hooks stay read-only, and commands reach the network only through
  agentty's proxy (private ranges and cloud metadata refused) — or not at
  all under None. Where the kernel is too old to keep a promise, the
  command is refused with the reason. The startup banner now names any wall
  this host could not build, and --sandbox on refuses to start if the
  configured posture cannot be built. A new CI job runs the sandbox's attack
  tests on every push with user namespaces disabled.
Fixed
- The cache gauge works on every provider, not just Anthropic. It was
  only armed by an event that OpenAI-compatible hosts (OpenRouter, DeepSeek,
  Groq, …) and Ollama never send, so on those it stayed blank.
- A provider that reports cached_tokens: 0 every turn now shows miss,
  not n/a. Zero counts were mistaken for "doesn't report a cache".
- Ollama's cache is counted. Ollama 0.40+ reports
  prompt_eval_cached_count; it was ignored, so every local cache hit read
  as fresh input. DeepSeek's prompt_cache_hit_tokens and a top-level
  cached_tokens are read too.
- Stats → Tokens "In" counts the whole prompt. It showed only the
  uncached part, so on a warm session "In" and "Total" read several times
  too low.
- Turns from a host with no cache no longer drag down the hit rate. A
  thread that switched providers counted those prompts as cache misses.
